Three hours, one page: your Product Vision Board, step by step.

This page shows what your team does in the 2-hour Team Studio and the 1-hour Home Sprint of Lab 01. Every step has a short animation of the move, the minutes it gets, what "done" looks like, and a note on what may look different on your screen. The full lab, the 2-page brief and the D2 template are downloadable at the bottom.

Tools are open

Every tool or technique shown on this page is a starting point. Swap it for any other that is suitable and available to your team, research it before you rely on it, and feel free to create your own. The animations use generic drawings, not any product's screens — what you see in your tool will be arranged differently; the words and the actions are the same.

Click a step's header to fold or unfold it; the round button at the bottom right folds or unfolds all. Every animation loops; download it if you want it on your own board.

OVERVIEWYour three hours: the 1 · 2 · 1 rhythm3 h max
  • 1 h lecture — the input: Waterfall vs Agile, the four values, the twelve principles, Denning's three laws. Not counted as lab work.
  • 2 h Team Studio (in class) — Planning 10' · Build 90' (Step 1 40' · Step 2 30' · Step 3 20') · Sprint Review 15' · Retrospective 5'.
  • 1 h Home Sprint — Polish 25' · Denning paragraph 15' · three checks and one cold read 10' · export and submit 10'.
  • Brick D2 — Product Vision Board, one page, due Sunday, October 4, 2026, 23:59 on Blackboard. Each member submits the team PDF (Portable Document Format) and their own Learning Log.
  • Denning Chapter 2 and the Learning Log are the weekly routine of every brick, outside the three hours.

Done when: The goal of the day is written; everyone knows the four boxes of the clock.

Version note (checked September 2026): dates are those of the 2026–2027 run of DIG 123 (Class 2 on Monday, September 28, 2026); deadlines change only by an announcement on Blackboard, which prevails over this page.

TOOLSTools are open — choose, research, or create your own10' per tool

Every tool named in this lab is a starting point, never a rule. Swap any of them for a tool that is suitable and available to your team — a different board, a whiteboard, a spreadsheet, sticky notes photographed with a phone, or something you build yourselves (a Markdown file with a Mermaid — mermaid.js.org timeline is a perfectly good vision board). Be creative, and research the tool before you commit.

  1. Official site only — never a mirror, a "download manager" or a search-engine ad.
  2. Free-tier limits — boards, members, files, storage.
  3. Licence / Terms of Use — may a student team use it, and what happens to your data? (Legal Notice §6.6 and §14)
  4. Scan the link — VirusTotal — virustotal.com and Google Safe Browsing — transparencyreport.google.com; a clean result is never a guarantee (Annex C).
  5. Try it five minutes with the whole team, then decide. Write the tools you chose in the D2 footer.

Starting points (official sites): boards — Trello · GitHub Projects · Jira · Focalboard · Wekan · Kanboard · Taiga; whiteboards — Excalidraw · tldraw · draw.io · Miro · FigJam · Penpot; files — Google Drive · OneDrive · LibreOffice.

Done when: You can name your tools, their free-tier limits and where their terms of use are.

Version note (checked September 2026): Trello Free — up to 10 boards and 10 collaborators per Workspace, unlimited cards, 10 MB (megabytes) per attachment. Jira Free — up to 10 users, 2 GB (gigabytes) of storage. Miro Free — only the 3 most recent boards stay editable. Figma Starter (free) — unlimited files in Drafts, co-editing on up to 3 files; students may apply for the Figma Education plan. Excalidraw, tldraw and draw.io — free, no account needed for basic use. GitHub Projects — included in GitHub Free. Free tiers and screens change often: if a menu is named differently from what you expect, look for the same action, not the same word.

STEP 0Planning — open D1, write the goal, give out the hats10'
  1. Open your D1 (Team Charter & Product Idea Card). D2 is built on it — same team, same product, same users.
  2. The Scribe writes the goal at the top of the template: "Product Vision v1 and an Agile fit check for [product], on one page."
  3. Give out the four hats — Facilitator, Timekeeper, Scribe, Presenter — and write the names in the footer. Rotate them every Monday.
  4. The Timekeeper sets 40 minutes for Step 1 and says "go". Planning ends at minute 10 whether or not you feel ready.

Done when: Goal on the page; hats given; template open; clock running.

STEP 1The vision sentence (20') — then users and needs (20')40'

1a · Vision sentence. Template: For [target users] who [need / situation], [Product] is a [category] that [key benefit]. Unlike [the alternative they use today], our product [the differentiator].

  • Minutes 0–8 — write alone, in silence. Four sentences, not one loud one.
  • Minutes 8–16 — read aloud and merge. The Scribe keeps the best answer per blank; the Facilitator settles each disagreement in one minute.
  • Minutes 16–20 — cold-read test. A member of the neighbouring team reads it once: can they say who it is for and why that person would use it? The blank that confused them is the one to fix.

Watch the usual mistakes: "everyone" in the For blank; a feature hiding in the who blank; "platform" as the category; a list of features as the benefit; "unlike nothing".

Done when: A stranger repeats the sentence in one breath and names the user and the reason.

Version note (checked September 2026): the six-blank template dates from 1991 (Geoffrey Moore, Crossing the Chasm); any equivalent template that yields the same six answers is accepted.

STEP 1bThree target users and the top-3 needs20'
  • Minutes 0–10 — three user cards. From D1's "who has that problem", three types of users: an invented first name and role, the situation in one line, the exact moment the problem hits. Composites, never real people — no real names or details of anyone outside the team on the board (Legal Notice §6.7, §20).
  • Minutes 10–20 — the top-3 needs. A need is a situation the user wants to get out of; a feature is one way to get them out. "Find a seat before the next class starts" is a need; "a map with filters" is a feature. If a line mentions a screen, a button or a notification, rewrite it.

Done when: Three cards exist and none of the three needs names a feature.

STEP 2Two plans, one product — Waterfall vs Agile on the same 12 weeks30'
  • 2a · Waterfall (10'). Five phases in sequence with realistic weeks. Write on the line: the week a real user first uses something (a survey is not use), the riskiest assumption of the Requirements phase, and the week Waterfall would discover it is wrong.
  • 2b · Agile (12'). Your first three increments, each the smallest usable slice: a name, "a user can [verb] …", and how you get feedback (who, how many, how). Star the week of each. Write the first-use week and the week the same assumption is caught. "Set up the database" is not an increment — nobody can use it.
  • 2c · Compare (8'). Box 5: the two first-contact dates, the two star counts, the two "caught in week …", and one risk line — what happens to each team if the assumption is wrong.

Done when: Box 5 has two dates, two star counts, two catch-weeks and a risk line; Box 3 has three increments a person could use that day.

Version note (checked September 2026): the weeks in the animation belong to the example product (increments in weeks 3, 6 and 9); use your own realistic durations. In a Waterfall plan the honest first-use week is the release week.

STEP 3Manifesto map — four values, four filmable practices20'

Five minutes per value. For each one, one practice your team will really do this semester. The filming test: could someone film your team doing it on a Monday? A practice has a day, a time, a place or channel, and a length. "We will communicate well" cannot be filmed; "three-minute stand-up in our chat, Monday, Wednesday and Friday at 18:00" can.

  • Individuals and interactions over processes and tools — when and where do we actually talk?
  • Working product over comprehensive documentation — what do we show at every Sprint Review?
  • Customer collaboration over contract negotiation — which real user sees the newest increment, how often?
  • Responding to change over following a plan — who may change the plan, when, and how fast?

Read the four values in the original: Manifesto for Agile Software Development — agilemanifesto.org (values) and agilemanifesto.org/principles.html (the twelve principles).

Done when: All four practices pass the filming test; at least two name a day of the week.

Version note (checked September 2026): the Manifesto's text has not changed since February 2001; the site's appearance may. The authors allow copying only in its entirety with their notice — this page paraphrases and links instead.

REVIEW + RETROSprint Review (15') and Retrospective (5')20'
  • Sprint Review. Each Presenter says the vision sentence and Increment 1 — nothing else — in 90 seconds, timed by the class Timekeeper. No slides, no demo. One question per team from the class. Then one vote each for the clearest vision. The Scribe writes the question and the vote in the D2 footer.
  • Retrospective. Three columns — start / stop / continue — one sticky note per person per column, about how the team worked today, not about the product. No discussion; photograph the wall; the three most repeated notes go into the footer.
  • End of studio at 120 minutes. Behind? Hand in what is on the page — the Home Sprint finishes it. Nothing new starts at home.

Done when: Footer has the review question, the vote and three retro notes.

HOMEHome Sprint (60') — polish, paragraph, checks, submit60'
  1. Polish (25'). One page; the same names in every box; every increment starts with a verb; footer complete (hats, tools, review question and vote, retro notes, changes since D1, AI (Artificial Intelligence) tools used for spelling / none). tutor.com is free for every student through Blackboard and reviews writing at any hour.
  2. Denning paragraph (15'). Five to seven sentences: one law (Small Team · Customer · Network), what it claims, two facts about your own product that show why the product needs it, and why the other two matter less right now.
  3. Three checks + one cold read (10'). (1) a stranger repeats the sentence in one breath; (2) every increment has a named user and a verb; (3) every practice can be filmed. Then one member reads the page cold and marks where they stumbled.
  4. Export, name, submit (10'). One PDF: DIG123_D2_<TeamName>_2026-10-04.pdf. Blackboard → DIG 123 → Assignments → D2 — Product Vision Board. Each member submits the team PDF and their own Learning Log (five lines: did · learned · surprised me · one question · one thing to apply). Keep your own copy — the Mid-Term on November 16 is written from your own D1–D7.

Deadline: Sunday, October 4, 2026, 23:59. Late: −10 % per day, three days maximum, then 0 — submit anyway. Missing Learning Log: −50 % of this brick for that student.

Done when: PDF submitted by every member with their own Learning Log; a personal copy saved.

What the finished page contains

Five boxes and a paragraph, on one page — the D2 template has the exact layout.

Box 1 · Vision sentence

The six blanks, plus who did the cold read and what they could not repeat.

Box 2 · Users and needs

Three invented user cards; three needs written as situations, never features.

Box 3 · First three increments

Week · name · "a user can [verb] …" · feedback from whom and how.

Box 4 · Manifesto map

One filmable practice per value: day, time, place or channel, length.

Box 5 · Two plans

Waterfall vs Agile: first real-user contact, feedback moments, the risky assumption and the week it is caught, one risk line.

The Denning paragraph + footer

Five to seven sentences on the law your product needs most; hats, tools, review question and vote, retro notes.
